newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU advisory committee backs Commission Boeing decision.
newsitem.headline: EU advisory committee backs Commission Boeing decision.

text.p: European antitrust experts gave their approval on Friday to the merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp , clearing the way for final EU blessing next week of the $15 billion deal.
The Commission said in a statement one representative in the experts' committee, which has only an advisory role, had expressed reservations.

"A majority of the advisory committee agrees with the Commission that the package of commitments offered by Boeing is sufficient to remedy the competition problems identified and prevents the strengthening of Boeing's dominant position," the late statement said.

The European Commission, the EU's competition watchdog, gave its preliminary approval on Wednesday after Boeing, the U.S. aircraft giant, agreed a number of last-minute concessions aimed at reducing the deal's anti-competitive effect in Europe.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin was reserved earlier on Friday about the deal, arguing that the Commission had been too quick in signalling approval and saying he would have to see what the concessions meant and whether they would be effective.

European research chief Edith Cresson, one of two French members of the Commission, also said she disagreed with the preliminary ruling arguing that the concessions, although not negligible, would not prevent Boeing from acquiring a near or total monopoly in some markets.

"Beyond the position it will have in large capacity planes, Boeing is acquiring a monopoly in 100-seater craft and a virtual monopoly, 90 percent of the world market, in freight transport planes," she was quoted by paper Le Monde.
The Commission has the power to take a final decision, which it intends to do at its last regular meeting on July 30 before it breaks for the August holiday. It needs only a majority vote.

The merger, which was announced in December, creates the world's largest aerospace company and allows Boeing to rely less heavily on the commercial aviation sector. McDonnell Douglas makes mainly military planes.
Boeing's share of the commercial jets market will increase to 70 percent from 64 percent at present, leaving only European consortium Airbus Industrie to compete with it.

The merged company is expected to generate $49 billion in revenue this year, of which 61 percent would come from commercial jets. Without the acquisition, Boeing would have $34.7 billion in revenue this year, with 76 percent coming from the commercial side.
The Seattle-based company has pledged not to enforce exclusivity provisions in controversial long-term supply contracts with AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Airlines.
It also agreed not to conclude any new exclusive aircraft supply contracts with airlines before August 1, 2007, after the Commission threatened to block the deal.
The fight between Boeing and the Commission took the two sides of the Atlantic to the brink of potentially damaging trade war.
